strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MOSES, GuacaMol, and the newly proposed NPGen), with results averaged over three runs and standard deviations reported in the appendix, which exceeds the typical rigor in this sub-field.

The paper addresses a genuine limitation of existing atom-based diffusion/flow models: scalability with molecule size and low-step sampling. The fragment-level representation yields strong empirical gains in validity, FCD, and few-step sampling (e.g., ~96.8% validity and 0.92 FCD at only 10 steps, outperforming atom-based baselines at 500 steps), and sampling-time comparisons (Table 9) are a nice addition.

The stochastic fragment bag strategy with Info-NCE parameterization is a sensible solution to the intractable fragment vocabulary problem, and the theoretical material (CTMC rate construction, detailed-balance augmentation, CFM-as-diffusion-bridge derivation in A.3.2) is mostly careful.

The proposed NPGen benchmark fills a real gap: standard benchmarks saturate, and the NP-specific metrics (NP-likeness KL, NPClassifier pathway/superclass/class KL) are well-motivated by drug discovery relevance, with a clear statistical comparison against MOSES/GuacaMol in appendix D.

The conditional generation study is thorough (classifier guidance + fragment bag reweighting, MAE-FCD trade-off analysis across simple properties and docking scores), and the ablations on sampling steps, unseen fragment bags, and autoencoder reconstruction accuracy are informative.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core methodology combines existing components (DFM via CTMC from Campbell et al. [32], Info-NCE from van den Oord et al. [44], classifier guidance following DiGress [3], BRICS fragmentation, a KL-regularized autoencoder). The fragment-based hierarchical generation idea is also well-explored by JT-VAE, HierVAE, and motif-based diffusion works; the contribution is more of a well-engineered integration than a fundamentally new technique.

The claim of 'superior performance' needs qualification: FragFM's novelty on MOSES is notably worse (87.1 vs. 95.0–99.9 for baselines), which is a well-known symptom of fragment-based models exploiting the training fragment vocabulary. The scaffold-split handling is somewhat ad hoc — the main-table Scaf result is weak and the remedy (sampling from test-set fragment bags) uses information unavailable to a real deployment model, so the 'generalization' argument is not fully convincing.

The NPGen benchmark uses a random i.i.d. split and evaluates with surrogate models (NP-likeness score, NPClassifier). A model could partly satisfy these metrics by memorizing training fragments; a scaffold- or pathway-based split and an analysis of fragment overlap between training and generated molecules would substantially strengthen the benchmark's credibility as a measure of genuine generalization.

Some design choices and evidence gaps: no ablation over the bag size N or the detailed-balance hyperparameters (ηnode, ηedge) set empirically; the bag-independence assumption at sampling time (B drawn i.i.d. from marginal p1) is asserted but never quantified; fairness of baseline comparisons on NPGen is unclear since baselines (e.g., JT-VAE trained on RTX 2080 Ti with limited hyperparameter search) may be under-tuned for the larger, more complex NP domain.

Presentation issues reduce polish: Table 8 lists DiGress twice under the 500-step setting; typos ('norm clipping', 'detialed', 'asses', 'controlability'); the disconnected-component handling and maximum molecule size assumptions of the fragment decoder are not clearly discussed, and the claim of 'lossless' reconstruction coexists with a 97.6% graph-level accuracy on NPGen that is glossed over.

strengths: The hybrid discrete/continuous flow matching formulation (DFM for fragment types/edges, CFM for the latent vector) is carefully derived, and the appendix provides a reasonably rigorous treatment, including the connection between CFM and VE diffusion bridges.

The stochastic fragment-bag strategy with Info-NCE parameterization is a sensible way to scale fragment-level generation to very large fragment vocabularies without building the full transition matrix.

Experimental coverage is broad: MOSES, GuacaMol, sampling-step ablations, runtime comparisons, conditional generation with classifier guidance and fragment-bag reweighting, and autoencoder reconstruction fidelity are all reported.

The proposed NPGen benchmark addresses a real gap: existing benchmarks (MOSES, GuacaMol) are saturating and natural-product chemical space is underexplored; the dataset statistics in appendix D support that NPGen is genuinely different from existing benchmarks.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The framework is largely a composition of existing components: BRICS fragmentation, the DFM/CTMC formulation of Campbell et al., CFM for the latent vector, classifier guidance following Vignac et al., and Info-NCE for contrastive posterior approximation. Fragment-based coarse-to-fine generation is also well established (JT-VAE, HierVAE, MoLeR, Levy & Rector-Brooks [16], Chen et al. [17]). Yet the paper compares against neither of the two fragment-based diffusion methods it critiques in Section 2.2, which is a significant omission for a paper whose central claim is the superiority of fragment-level flow matching.

Concerning evaluation protocol on the scaffold split. FragFM performs notably worse than baselines on Novelty (87.1 vs. 92-99) and Scaffold (10.9 vs. 10-16) on MOSES. The 'fix' reported in Tables 6-7 regenerates molecules using fragment bags drawn from the test set. Allowing the generative model to sample from test-split fragments at inference time effectively circumvents the scaffold split and is not a valid comparison against baselines that never receive test information; this undermines the claimed generalization result rather than supporting it.

The near-lossless autoencoder (99%+ reconstruction accuracy) means the model's atom-level output is largely a reassembly of memorized training fragments, with the latent z encoding the discarded connectivity. It is unclear how much genuine molecular novelty the pipeline can produce versus recombining training fragments; the low novelty score on MOSES is consistent with this, but no analysis or ablation (e.g., fraction of novel fragments/scaffolds generated) is provided.

NPGen has methodological concerns: the COCONUT-derived dataset is split i.i.d. (no scaffold split), likely containing near-duplicates, which inflates distribution-matching metrics; the authors both propose the benchmark and tune their model on it, while baselines (e.g., GraphAF, JT-VAE with a Python 2 codebase) receive comparatively less tuning effort. Favorable benchmark results on a self-proposed benchmark provide weaker evidence than results on established ones.

Missing or insufficient ablations: no ablation on the fragment bag size N, the latent dimension, the guidance weights, or a fixed-fragment-library baseline that would isolate the benefit of the stochastic bag. Hyperparameters such as detailed-balance rates and guidance strengths (λ) are set differently across experiments (e.g., λ=20.0 in fig. 3, 0.5 in fig. 12, 0.1 in fig. 14) without justification, suggesting per-experiment tuning that weakens the fairness of cross-model comparisons.

The Info-NCE in-bag approximation introduces a train/sampling bias (the bag-conditioned posterior does not recover the true posterior), acknowledged only informally with an appeal to asymptotics; no empirical characterization of the bias vs. bag size is given.

Significance is moderate at best: atom-level flow/diffusion models are maturing rapidly, and the claimed scalability advantage is demonstrated only up to ~100 heavy atoms on MOSES/GuacaMol/NPGen; generation of truly large molecules (the stated motivation for fragment-level abstraction) is never actually shown.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, several implementation details are deferred to appendices that remain coarse (e.g., the GT architecture is only said to mirror prior work), and the manuscript contains copy-editing and consistency errors (duplicate references [20]/[51] and [68]/[72], 'gradient-nrom', 'detialed-balance', inconsistent appendix numbering F.1 appearing under section F labeled E.1/E.2/E.3) that suggest insufficient polish.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the paper addresses the scalability and chemical-validity limitations of atom-based discrete diffusion/flow models for molecular graphs by combining fragment-level discrete flow matching with a coarse-to-fine autoencoder that preserves lossless atom-level connectivity.

Technically sound and reasonably novel components: the stochastic fragment bag strategy with an Info-NCE parameterization cleverly avoids the intractable |F|-sized transition matrix, and the hybrid discrete-flow (nodes/edges) + continuous-flow (latent z) formulation, including the VE-diffusion-bridge analysis connecting CFM to their kernel, is well developed in the appendix.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: state-of-the-art or near-SOTA results on MOSES and GuacaMol against strong recent one-shot baselines (DiGress, DisCo, Cometh, DeFoG), a thorough sampling-step ablation showing strong robustness at very few denoising steps, runtime comparisons, unseen-fragment-bag experiments, and conditional generation experiments with classifier guidance and bag reweighting.

The proposed NPGen benchmark (built from COCONUT with NP-likeness and NPClassifier-based KL divergence metrics) is a genuinely useful community contribution that addresses saturation of MOSES/GuacaMol metrics and is well characterized against existing benchmarks.
Reconstruction fidelity of the coarse-to-fine autoencoder is quantified (Table 5), and qualitative chemical analysis of generated molecules across models adds credibility to the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: Missing comparison with directly relevant fragment-based generative methods: the related work discusses Levy & Rector-Brooks [16] and Chen et al. [17] (BPE-based fragmentation) and motif-based methods (MARS, MoLeR, MAGNet), yet none of these appear in the experimental tables. Without at least one such baseline, the claim that the fragment-based approach 'consistently outperforms previous graph generative models' is only demonstrated against atom-based one-shot models.

Low novelty score (87.1) on MOSES relative to all baselines raises a partial-memorization concern inherent to fragment recombination; the paper acknowledges this only indirectly, and there is no diversity analysis (e.g., internal diversity, fragment usage statistics of generated molecules) to substantiate that FragFM is not merely reassembling training fragments.

The scaffold-split limitation is a structural weakness of the method on the standard MOSES protocol: the test-set-fragment-bag experiment (Table 6) is informative but arguably changes the evaluation setting; the fair comparison issue deserves more careful discussion in the main text rather than a caveat.

Some methodological approximations are informally justified: the in-bag transition kernel is a surrogate whose quality depends on bag size N, but there is no ablation on N (bag size), latent dimension, or sensitivity to the guidance hyperparameters; the smoothness assumption for guidance (eq. 31-32) is inherited from prior work rather than validated.

The novelty of individual components is moderate: fragment/motif-based generation, CTMC-based discrete flow matching, Info-NCE-based large-vocabulary handling, and classifier guidance are all established; the contribution is primarily a well-engineered combination, which limits the conceptual depth relative to the framing.
No explicit statement about code/data release for the NPGen benchmark or the model, which affects reproducibility, particularly for a proposed new community benchmark.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'lossless' reconstruction is not exact (97-99% accuracy), and the superiority on NPGen could partly reflect fragment vocabulary coverage of COCONUT rather than better structural modeling; ablations isolating the fragment-bag component's contribution on standard benchmarks are absent.

strengths: Well-motivated framework that addresses a real scalability bottleneck of atom-level discrete diffusion/flow models by operating at the fragment level, combining masked DFM (Campbell et al.) with a stochastic fragment-bag strategy via Info-NCE that avoids a fixed, small fragment vocabulary and scales to very large fragment libraries (~190k fragments in GuacaMol).

Strong empirical results across multiple established benchmarks (MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k), with near-SOTA FCD, near-100% validity, and large gains in sampling efficiency (e.g., robust quality at 10-50 steps, ~5x faster than DiGress on NPGen).

Introduction of NPGen, a new benchmark built from COCONUT with careful dataset construction, NP-specific metrics (NP-likeness KL, NPClassifier pathway/superclass/class KL), and thorough documentation—this is a useful community contribution addressing benchmark saturation.

Extensive ablations and analyses: autoencoder reconstruction quality (including random-z ablation), fragment bag size effects (SNIS bias/variance discussion), long-tail fragment recovery, unseen-fragment generalization on scaffold-split MOSES, temperature knobs for novelty-fidelity trade-off, and detailed hyperparameter tables supporting reproducibility.

Conditional generation experiments go beyond simple properties (QED/logP/rings) to challenging docking-score conditioning in extreme-tail regions of ZINC250k, demonstrating the practical value of fragment-bag reweighting as an additional control mechanism.

Appendix theory is careful: the CFM-as-limiting-case-of-VE-bridge derivation and the guidance-ratio Taylor approximation are stated with their assumptions made explicit and consistent with prior discrete-guidance work.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate and largely compositional: masked DFM, Info-NCE-based posterior estimation, classifier guidance, and BRICS fragmentation (as in JT-VAE) are all existing components; the paper's contribution is their integration rather than a fundamentally new generative principle. The in-bag transition kernel (eq. 3) is a heuristic surrogate whose distributional correctness is argued only informally (convergence as N→|F|, SNIS behavior), with no error bounds or analysis of the induced bias on the learned data distribution.

Fragment-based one-shot baselines are missing from the main comparisons (e.g., MoFlow and other motif/fragment-level one-shot models); the fragment-level comparison is dominated by autoregressive VAEs (JT-VAE, HierVAE), making it hard to isolate whether gains come from the framework itself or merely from fragment-level representation. Similarly, comparisons on NPGen include only one one-shot baseline (DiGress).

The per-molecule latent vector z must capture all inter-fragment connectivity for lossless reconstruction; its generative modeling quality is not directly analyzed (only autoencoder reconstruction is reported). Reconstruction-collapsed or mode-restricted behavior of the FM-generated z could silently degrade chemical plausibility, and the paper relies mostly on aggregate metrics to rule this out.

Known weaknesses of the approach on MOSES Scaf and Novelty are explained but only partially mitigated; the novelty-vs-fidelity trade-off and the reliance on test-set fragment bags (table 8) somewhat qualify the headline claims, and a reviewer may view the novelty explanation as partially self-serving.

Some experimental details raise minor fairness questions: baselines retrained with limited or default hyperparameter searches, differing hardware for timing comparisons (RTX 3090 vs. A100 for DeFoG numbers), and guidance-strength calibration between FragFM and DiGress that requires manual tuning to reach 'comparable FCD'.

Writing/notation has small inconsistencies (e.g., G vs. G-cursive usage in the overview, minor typos such as 'a particularly important', 'independent to', 'parameteres'), and the code release status is not explicitly stated, which limits immediate reproducibility despite the extensive appendix.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the FragFM framework is well-motivated: fragment-level discrete flow matching with a stochastic fragment bag (Info-NCE formulation) is a sensible solution to the large-vocabulary problem that limits prior fragment-based diffusion models.

Experiments are broad and generally convincing: consistent state-of-the-art or near-SOTA results on MOSES, GuacaMol, and ZINC250k against a large set of recent baselines (DiGress, DisCo, Cometh, DeFoG, SAFE-GPT), with substantial FCD improvements (e.g., 0.58 on MOSES vs 1.00+ for prior work).
The NPGen benchmark is a genuine contribution; the dataset construction, NP-specific metrics (NP-likeness KL, NPClassifier divergences), and dataset statistics are documented in reasonable detail.

Several useful analyses support the design choices: autoencoder reconstruction ablations (Table 6/7), fragment bag size ablations, long-tail fragment recovery, temperature-based novelty control, and sampling-step efficiency (strong quality at only 10-50 steps).

Conditional generation experiments, including a challenging JAK2 docking-score task at the extreme tail of the distribution, demonstrate practical controllability beyond standard unconditional benchmarks.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily architectural/engineering integration rather than a new generative principle: the components (masked DFM/CTMC from Campbell et al., CFM from Lipman et al., Info-NCE negative sampling, latent two-stage generation as in latent diffusion, BRICS fragmentation, Blossom matching) are all established, and the paper does not clearly isolate which combination yields the gains. No ablation comparing against, e.g., a fixed-vocabulary DFM at equal compute.

The theoretical justification for the stochastic fragment bag is thin: the claim that the bag-conditioned kernel 'converges to the exact one as N approaches |F|' is trivial, the Taylor-expansion argument in eq. (28) assumes bag distributions vary continuously with X without justification, and the actual gap at N=384 vs. vocabulary sizes of ~40k-193k (Section D.2) is never quantified empirically.

Unfavorable results are downplayed: novelty on MOSES (87.1 vs 95-99 for baselines) and scaffold similarity are among the weakest, and the scaffold recovery 'fix' (Section C.3) uses fragment bags drawn from the test split, which arguably leaks test information and weakens that claim.

The NPGen benchmark comparisons omit the most relevant recent fragment-based one-shot methods (e.g., the BPE-fragment diffusion of Chen et al. 2024 discussed at length in Related Works), so the headline NPGen advantage is only demonstrated against one-shot atom-based DiGress and older autoregressive fragment VAEs; the NP-oriented KL metrics may also structurally favor fragment-based generators by construction.

Information flow between the autoencoder and the flow model is not fully examined: z is encoded from the ground-truth atom graph during training but must be generated jointly at sampling time; there is no analysis of reconstruction degradation as a function of the flow-generated z quality (only the random-z ablation, which is an extreme case).

Guidance and conditional experiments are compared almost exclusively against DiGress, and some timing comparisons mix results from original papers on different hardware (Table 12), complicating the efficiency claims.
Missing details hurt reproducibility: no explicit statement of code/data release for FragFM or the NPGen benchmark despite the benchmark being offered as a community resource.

strengths: The core methodological contribution is well-motivated: the stochastic fragment bag strategy (Info-NCE-based density ratio estimation over an in-bag candidate set) is a clean and effective solution to the otherwise prohibitive fragment vocabulary size problem in discrete flow matching, and the coarse-to-fine autoencoder with Blossom-based discretization provides a principled path from fragment-level to atom-level graphs with >97-99% reconstruction accuracy.

Comprehensive evaluation across MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k, and the newly proposed NPGen benchmark, against a broad set of competitive baselines spanning autoregressive and one-shot, atom- and fragment-level methods (JT-VAE, HierVAE, SAFE-GPT, DiGress, DisCo, Cometh, DeFoG, GraphAF).

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art FCD on MOSES/GuacaMol/ZINC250k, near-perfect validity without explicit validity constraints, >5x faster sampling than DiGress on NPGen, and robust performance at very low sampling step counts (e.g., competitive at 10-50 steps).

NPGen is a valuable community contribution: it is substantially larger (658K molecules, avg. 35 heavy atoms) and structurally distinct from MOSES/GuacaMol, with domain-grounded NP-specific metrics (NP-likeness KL, NPClassifier pathway/superclass/class KL), and the dataset construction/filtering is transparently documented.

Thorough ablations and analyses: autoencoder reconstruction (including random-z ablation), fragment bag size effects for training vs. inference, long-tail fragment recovery, unseen-fragment generalization, temperature scaling for novelty control, conditional generation with dual guidance (lambda_X and lambda_B), and detailed hyperparameter tables supporting reproducibility.

Theoretical treatment is reasonably careful: the in-bag kernel is honestly presented as a practical surrogate converging to the exact kernel as N -> |F|, and the CFM-as-VE-bridge-limit connection is clearly derived.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the framework combines largely known components (masked DFM/CTMC, continuous flow matching, Info-NCE negative sampling, coarse-to-fine autoencoders in the style of latent diffusion), and the paper itself concedes the contribution is primarily a framework rather than architectural novelty.

The bag-conditioned transition kernel introduces a train/inference mismatch (posterior over the restricted bag vs. the true unconditional posterior), and the justification relies on the convergence argument as N approaches |F| plus the claim that the discrepancy is 'negligible' at moderate N; a more rigorous quantification of this approximation error would strengthen the work.

Two-stage pipeline error compounding is only partially addressed: autoencoder reconstruction is near-perfect on training/test distributions, but its behavior on out-of-distribution fragment graphs produced by the flow model is not directly measured, which is the regime that matters during generation.

Novelty on MOSES (87.1) is notably lower than atom-based baselines (95.0-97.7) and even fragment-based JT-VAE (99.9); the mitigation via temperature scaling trades off fidelity (FCD degrades from 0.58 to 0.91), and the framing that higher novelty 'does not always guarantee better quality' partially deflects a legitimate concern.

Conditional generation comparisons are limited to DiGress; the guidance experiments would be more convincing with additional guided baselines (e.g., guided DeFoG/Cometh or autoregressive property optimization methods).

NPGen's evaluation depends heavily on NPClassifier/NP-likeness-based KL divergences, which are themselves learned tools and may correlate with substructure recombination bias in fragment-level models; a broader diversity/validity analysis for NP-like scaffolds would help preempt concerns that fragment-based methods exploit the metric.
No explicit statement of code or benchmark release is given in the main text, which limits reproducibility and community adoption of NPGen despite its stated goal of serving the field.

Minor presentation issues (e.g., inconsistent hyperparameter values between appendix sections, typos such as 'Droptout', minor table formatting in Table 11) and some reliance on assumptions borrowed from prior guidance work that are stated rather than re-validated.

strengths: Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: FragFM is benchmarked on MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k, and a newly introduced NPGen dataset against a broad set of autoregressive and one-shot baselines (JT-VAE, HierVAE, SAFE-GPT, MolHF, DiGress, DeFoG, Cometh, DisCo), with SOTA or near-SOTA results on most fidelity metrics (e.g., FCD 0.58 on MOSES, five-fold NSPDK improvement on ZINC250k).

The stochastic fragment bag strategy via Info-NCE is a well-motivated solution to the large-vocabulary problem in fragment-based generative modeling, and the loss scaling argument (cost O(N) instead of O(|F|)) is clearly presented; ablations on bag size (N_train vs N_inference) sensibly frame the estimator-variance trade-off.

The coarse-to-fine autoencoder is well analyzed: over 99% bond-level reconstruction accuracy, ablations with random z and randomized decoder, and demonstrations of generalization to unseen test-set fragments (large Scaf score gains) — these support the design choices empirically.

NPGen is a useful community contribution: motivated construction from COCONUT with clear filtering criteria, NP-specific metrics (NP-likeness KL, NPClassifier pathway/superclass/class KL), detailed dataset statistics distinguishing it from MOSES/GuacaMol, and full baselines with error bars over three runs.

Additional analyses strengthen the claims: retrosynthetic feasibility via AIZynthFinder, long-tail fragment recovery, sampling-step robustness (strong quality at 10–50 steps vs. baselines needing 500), and joint fragment-bag + classifier guidance including a challenging docking-score task in an extreme tail region.

Thorough reproducibility: full hyperparameter tables, implementation details for all baselines (including retraining SAFE-GPT and adjusting GraphAF/JT-VAE/HierVAE for NPGen), and extensive qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the framework is largely a careful combination of existing components (masked DFM/CTMC from Campbell et al., continuous CFM from Lipman et al., classifier guidance from Vignac et al., BRICS fragmentation, Info-NCE negative sampling). The primary contribution is system-level design and benchmarking rather than a new generative principle; the in-bag transition kernel (eq. 3) is acknowledged as an approximation but only informally justified (SNIS bias/variance discussion is qualitative, with no error bounds or empirical study of the approximation error itself).

Some claims are slightly overclaimed: the abstract states reconstruction is 'without information loss', yet the autoencoder compresses connectivity into a latent z with KL regularization and finite graph-level accuracy (97.4% on NPGen); 'lossless' is not literally true.

The Blossom-based decoder enforces deg_M(v) <= 1 on junction-atom matchings, which may not faithfully represent all multi-bond junction configurations; the paper does not discuss cases where this matching constraint loses valid atom-level graphs, and reconstruction errors (2.4–2.6% of graphs on NPGen/ZINC250k) propagate silently into generation.

Conditional-generation comparisons are against only one baseline (DiGress); no comparison to fragment-based conditional baselines (e.g., HierVAE goal-directed variants or SAFE-based steering), making the claim of 'controllability unattainable in purely atomistic approaches' less thoroughly supported.

Baseline hyperparameters on NPGen were largely default settings tuned for small drug-like datasets (e.g., DiGress/DeFoG), so the large gaps on NPGen may partly reflect suboptimal baselines rather than a fundamental atom-level limitation; a sensitivity study of atom-based baselines on NPGen would strengthen the claim.

Novelty on MOSES/GuacaMol is comparatively weak (87.1% vs. ~95–99% for atom-based baselines); the proposed mitigation (temperature scaling) is a sampling heuristic rather than a modeling fix, and the fidelity–novelty framing is asserted more than quantified.
The derivation in Appendix A.3 relies on smoothness/Taylor-expansion assumptions adopted from prior work without empirical verification of the guidance-ratio approximation error.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four datasets (MOSES, GuacaMol, ZINC250k, NPGen) with many recent strong baselines (DiGress, DeFoG, Cometh, DisCo, SAFE-GPT), multi-run averages, and extensive ablations (fragmentation rules, bag sizes, sampling steps, decoder ablation, long-tail fragment recovery, retrosynthetic analysis).

The proposed NPGen benchmark is a useful community contribution: it is well-motivated (existing benchmarks are saturating and drug-like only), constructed transparently from COCONUT, and comes with domain-relevant evaluation metrics (NP-likeness KL, NPClassifier pathway/superclass/class KL).

The technical framing is reasonably well executed: the in-bag transition kernel via Info-NCE is a principled way to scale DFM to large fragment vocabularies, and the appendix provides the CTMC rate derivations and the guidance-ratio approximation.

The conditional generation experiments (joint fragment-bag and classifier guidance, docking-score conditioning on a rare region of ZINC250k) demonstrate a genuinely useful extra degree of controllability, and the sampling-efficiency results (robust at 10-50 steps, ~5x faster than DiGress on NPGen) are convincing.

The ablations are unusually thorough: the random-z and random-decoder ablations (tables 8-9) explicitly isolate the roles of the latent vector and pre-trained decoder, which strengthens the mechanistic claims.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest: the framework is largely a combination of existing components—masked DFM (Campbell et al., 2024), Info-NCE negative sampling over a large vocabulary, a VAE-style coarse-to-fine autoencoder, and a combinatorial matching step (Blossom)—applied to fragment-level generation. The paper itself concedes the primary contribution is a framework rather than architectural or algorithmic novelty.

The claim of 'superior performance' on NPGen is overstated. In table 2, SAFE-GPT substantially outperforms FragFM on nearly every distributional metric (NP Score KL 0.0024 vs 0.0374; NPClassifier KLs; FCD 0.15 vs 1.34). FragFM is only the best among *graph-based* models; the abstract and section 5.2 blur this distinction.

The in-bag transition kernel is an approximation whose bias relative to the exact kernel is never quantified; the claim that the discrepancy is 'negligible' is asserted rather than measured (e.g., no experiment comparing bag-conditioned vs. exact small-vocabulary kernels).

The fragment-bag reweighting for conditional generation relies on several stacked heuristics (Taylor expansion of bag distributions, Gaussian noisy predictor, fixed variance) without analysis of when the approximation degrades; only empirical trade-off curves are shown.

The coarse-to-fine autoencoder is trained once and frozen; this architecture plausibly constrains generation to compositions of training fragments and contributes to the weak novelty (87.1 on MOSES) and scaffold scores. The 'test fragment bag' experiment (C.4) is a diagnostic rather than a fix and borders on using test-set information.

Apples-to-apples fairness concerns: FragFM reconstructs via a 99%+ accurate autoencoder trained on the full dataset, effectively amortizing part of the modeling task into the decoder; it is unclear how much of the FCD/validity advantage over atom-based baselines stems from this pre-trained reconstruction module versus the flow model itself. The random-decoder ablation partially addresses but does not fully resolve this.

Property predictors for guidance are trained on the full labeled dataset for both models, but docking-based conditioning is evaluated only against DiGress as a baseline; stronger goal-directed baselines or retrieval-augmented fragment methods (e.g., Lee et al., 2024, cited but not compared) are absent.

Scalability of the single continuous latent vector z encoding all inter-fragment connectivity is questionable for very large molecules; the NPGen evaluation caps at 99 heavy atoms, and behavior near the upper end (or beyond) is not analyzed.

Some presentation issues: the equivalence between CFM and the VE diffusion bridge (A.2.3) is tangential to the main contribution; key approximation assumptions in the guidance ratio are spread across appendix A.3; and the novelty-vs-fidelity discussion in the main text could be more direct about the model's weaker novelty on standard benchmarks.

strengths: Well-motivated approach: the stochastic fragment bag strategy elegantly scales discrete flow matching to very large fragment vocabularies (|F| in the hundreds of thousands), with a clear Info-NCE formulation and an honest discussion of the approximation error (eq. 3 convergence as N → |F|).

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: SOTA or near-SOTA results on MOSES (FCD 0.58), GuacaMol, and ZINC250k against strong recent baselines (DiGress, DeFoG, Cometh, DisCo), averaged over three runs with standard deviations reported.

The NPGen benchmark is a genuinely useful community contribution: well-motivated (saturating MOSES/GuacaMol metrics), carefully constructed from COCONUT with documented filtering, and accompanied by NP-specific metrics (NP-likeness KL, NPClassifier KL at three hierarchy levels) and full baseline implementations.

Strong practical efficiency claims backed by data: ~5x faster sampling than DiGress on NPGen, robust quality at 10-50 denoising steps (table 13), which addresses the scalability critique motivating the work.

Unusually thorough ablations and analyses: autoencoder reconstruction accuracy (>99% bond accuracy, table 7-8), random-z and random-decoder controls, unseen-fragment generalization (tables 10-11), long-tail fragment recovery, bag-size ablations, fragmentation-rule robustness (table 3), temperature-based novelty trade-off (table 12), and retrosynthetic accessibility analysis (fig. 10).

Novel conditioning mechanism: property-steered fragment bag reweighting (λ_B) combined with standard classifier guidance provides controllability that atom-based baselines cannot replicate, demonstrated in a challenging docking-score regime (top 0.08% of ZINC250k).
Highly detailed appendices with complete derivations, hyperparameters, and baseline training details support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is primarily compositional: masked DFM, Info-NCE density-ratio estimation, coarse-to-fine autoencoders, and Blossom-based matching are all established components; the contribution is their combination and adaptation to fragment-level molecular generation rather than new generative theory.

The theoretical justification for the in-bag kernel is informal: the claim that the surrogate 'converges to the exact one as N approaches |F|' and that the discrepancy is 'negligible' for moderate N is heuristic; no bound on the bias of the SNIS estimator at N=384 versus |F|~40k-190k is provided, though the bag-size ablation (fig. 12) partially mitigates this concern.

FragFM underperforms on novelty (87.1% vs. 92-97% for atom-based baselines) and scaffold similarity on MOSES; the proposed remedies (temperature scaling, test-set fragment bags) are reasonable but partly sidestep the fundamental limitation that fixed fragmentation vocabularies constrain generation to training-fragment recombinations.

The NPGen benchmark comparisons may partially favor fragment-based methods by construction: baselines were run largely with default hyperparameters on a much larger and more complex dataset, and it is unclear how sensitive the atom-based baselines' poor results are to tuning.

Two-stage training (frozen autoencoder) means flow-matching errors in the coarse graph cannot be compensated by the decoder; the strong dependency on the encoder's latent z (table 8) raises questions about robustness when the generated coarse graph distribution drifts from training data, which is addressed only indirectly.

No comparison to other recent fragment-based diffusion approaches (e.g., Levy & Rector-Brooks, Chen et al. BPE-based fragmentation) on identical benchmarks, making it harder to isolate whether gains come from the fragment bag strategy specifically versus fragment-level representation generally.
Compute footprint is significant (96-144 GPU-hours per dataset on an A100), and no direct efficiency comparison of training time with baselines is given.
